Longfin smelt (Spirinchus thaleichthys) exhibit a delicate early life stage beginning with the fertilised ovum. Upon eclosion, the yolk-sac larva emerges, carrying a substantial endogenous nutritional supply. Field measurements indicate that the wet weight at birth is approximately 0.000449 grams [Wwb = approximately 0.000449 grams], a value derived from the average diameter of the demersal, adhesive eggs. These incubating eggs, measuring about 0.95 mm, are deposited in freshwater tributaries where development proceeds. The subsequent exotrophic transition occurs once the yolk reserves are exhausted, marking the onset of exogenous feeding. This delicate period is critical for recruitment as the prolarvae move downstream towards estuarine nursery grounds. Their small size makes them vulnerable to predation and environmental fluctuations, yet this initial mass represents a calculated energetic investment by the spawning adult that supports the larva through the first days of life until it can capture its first prey.

As the young-of-year grow and transition into the juvenile stage, their growth trajectory begins to define the species' life history strategy. The total length at puberty has been determined through examination of gonadal recrudescence in field-caught specimens, with individuals reaching this developmental milestone at 9 cm [Lp = 9 cm]. Correspondingly, the wet weight at puberty is recorded at 4 grams [Wwp = 4 grams], a mass that reflects the somatic investment required before reproductive activation can commence. First spawning typically occurs shortly after this size is attained, with males and females moving into spawning aggregations in the upper reaches of tidal rivers. The attainment of this length and weight is a reliable indicator that the HPG axis has been activated and that the individual is transitioning from an immature organism to a reproductively viable adult capable of participating in the annual spawning run.

Over the course of its life, the Longfin smelt continues somatic growth, though at a decelerating rate, until approaching an asymptotic size. The ultimate total length observed for this species is 20 cm [Li = 20 cm], a value consistent across much of its range from California to Alaska. The ultimate wet weight corresponding to this maximum size is approximately 50.3 grams [Wwi = approximately 50.3 grams], representing the heaviest individuals recorded in survey samples. These maximum values are typically attained by older, iteroparous adults that have survived multiple spawning seasons. Growth increments diminish considerably after the onset of reproduction, as energy is increasingly directed toward gametogenesis and spawning migrations rather than continued elongation. Consequently, very few individuals approach this upper size limit, as mortality from predation and the physiological demands of spawning imposes a strong selective pressure against extreme longevity.

The lifespan of Spirinchus thaleichthys under natural conditions is relatively short, characteristic of many osmerid fishes adapted to seasonal environments. Long-term monitoring of marked populations in San Francisco Bay tributaries reveals that maximum longevity is approximately 3 years [am = approximately 3 years], a duration measured under the thermal regime typical of these coastal systems, where water temperatures average 9 °C [T = 9 °C] during much of the growing season. This abbreviated life cycle is a classic feature of an annual or short-lived iteroparous species. Most individuals spawn for the first time at age one, and a smaller fraction return to spawn a second time at age two. Senescence and post-spawning mortality are pronounced, with very few fish surviving to a third winter. The cool water temperatures likely contribute to this relatively extended lifespan compared to more southerly osmerids, as lower metabolic rates may reduce the accumulation of oxidative damage.

Comparisons with other osmerid fishes highlight the moderately sized nature of Longfin smelt life history traits. The wet weight at puberty of 4 grams [Wwp = 4 grams] is intermediate between the smaller Delta smelt (Hypomesus transpacificus) and the larger Eulachon (Thaleichthys pacificus). Similarly, the total length at puberty of 9 cm [Lp = 9 cm] occurs well before the ultimate total length of 20 cm [Li = 20 cm] is approached, indicating a substantial period of post-maturational growth. The largest individuals, reaching an ultimate wet weight of 50.3 grams [Wwi = 50.3 grams], are rare in survey catches but provide important data for understanding the species' growth potential. The lifespan of about 3 years [am = about 3 years] at 9 °C [T = 9 °C] is consistent with the general pattern among osmerids, where cooler thermal regimes tend to correlate with greater longevity. These population-level parameters inform stock assessments and conservation planning for this species, which has experienced significant declines in portions of its range.
